title: Magnetism and induction
note: Magnetic fields come from moving charges and exert forces only on moving charges, at right angles to both the velocity and the field. A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an emf (Faraday's law), and the induced current opposes the change that caused it (Lenz's law).

read.title: Currents and changing fields
text: Magnets and electric currents turned out to be two faces of one phenomenon. In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a current in a wire deflects a compass needle. Every magnetic field comes from moving charge, whether a current in a wire or electrons spinning and orbiting inside iron.

A magnetic field pushes on a moving charge with a force qvB sin θ, perpendicular to both the velocity and the field. Because that force is always sideways, it does no work: it bends a charged particle into a circle without changing its speed. A current-carrying wire in a field feels the same push, and a loop of wire feels a torque. That torque spins every electric motor.

In 1831 Michael Faraday found the reverse effect. A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an emf, whether the magnet moves, the loop moves, or the field strength changes. Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced current creates a field that opposes the change. Generators turn mechanical rotation into electricity this way, and transformers use alternating current to step voltages up or down. Power companies send electricity at high voltage because the same power then needs less current, and resistive losses grow with the square of the current.
